source: Kuleshov & Precup (2014) Algorithms for the multi-armed bandit problem
finding: Large simulation of bandit algorithms finds the simple heuristics beat the provably good ones on most settings.
numbers: Abstract: epsilon-greedy and Boltzmann (softmax) beat theoretically sound algorithms on most settings by a significant margin. Softmax had lowest total regret on all tasks except high-variance (sigma=1) with K=2,5,10 arms, where UCB1-Tuned was best.
quote: simple heuristics such as epsilon-greedy and Boltzmann exploration outperform theoretically sound algorithms on most settings
limits: Simulated Bernoulli and Gaussian arms; parameters tuned per setting (epsilon from 0.005 to 0.1), so the win depends on tuning.
agent_relevance: Theory (UCB, Thompson) does not mean better in practice. A tuned simple per-class widen rule can match a fancier one; tune on our own per-class pass rates.

source: Kuleshov & Precup (2014) Algorithms for the multi-armed bandit problem
finding: Same study: each algorithm has settings where it works and settings where it fails, and theory does not predict which.
numbers: Abstract: performance of most algorithms varies dramatically with bandit parameters (arms K, variance, gap). Result tables give total regret per algorithm, e.g. epsilon-greedy eps=0.005 gave 1.21 on one setting.
quote: These properties are not described by current theory, even though they can be exploited in practice
limits: Regret depends on horizon and arm count; I read the abstract and result tables, not every figure.
agent_relevance: Do not import one exploration rule for all classes. Calibrate widen thresholds per class and re-check when the class mix changes.

source: Kuleshov & Precup (2014) Algorithms for the multi-armed bandit problem
finding: Clinical-trial simulation: bandit allocation still identifies the best treatment, but weaker algorithms give weaker significance.
numbers: Out-patient case (clonidine success only 5%): worst p-value 0.017, returned by epsilon-greedy. In-patient worst p-value 1.5e-4. Authors conclude bandit algorithms can reliably identify the best arm.
quote: bandit algorithms can reliably identify the best arm
limits: Simulation built from a real trial (Link 2005); dropout counted as failure.
agent_relevance: Cost-aware allocation still lets us confirm which class or branch is better; low base rates (5%) make confirmation hard, as with rare-pass task classes.

source: Russo, Van Roy, Kazerouni, Osband, Wen (2020) A Tutorial on Thompson Sampling
finding: Tutorial: epsilon-greedy wastes effort. It perturbs at random and keeps exploring actions already known to be bad.
numbers: Text says dithering (epsilon-greedy) wastes resources; worked 3-arm Bernoulli example with true means 0.9, 0.8, 0.7 where a greedy rule can lock onto a worse arm. Thompson sampling samples from the posterior, so exploration shrinks as certainty grows.
limits: Tutorial, not a new experiment. Gains over epsilon-greedy depend on a sensible prior.
agent_relevance: Random widening at a fixed rate is the weak baseline. A posterior-based rule (sample the pass-rate belief per class) spends fewer attempts on classes known to be dead.

source: Russo, Van Roy, Kazerouni, Osband, Wen (2020) A Tutorial on Thompson Sampling
finding: Thompson sampling needs a prior and a model; the tutorial covers priors, misspecification and practical limits.
numbers: Covers beta-Bernoulli (uniform prior alpha=beta=1), prior choice, misspecified models and non-stationarity; no single headline number.
limits: Guarantees assume the model family is right. LLM pass events are not independent draws (correlated errors, SCHEMA G4).
agent_relevance: Beta-Bernoulli per class is cheap and code-checked, matching the rule that the program decides. Pass events from one model are correlated, so shrink counts.

source: Kaufmann, Korda, Munos (2012) Thompson Sampling: an asymptotically optimal finite-time analysis
finding: First finite-time proof that Thompson sampling is asymptotically optimal for Bernoulli bandits.
numbers: Theorem 1: regret R(T) <= (1+eps) * sum over suboptimal arms of (mu* - mu_a)/KL(mu_a,mu*) * (ln T + ln ln T) + C(eps, mu). Matches the Lai-Robbins lower bound. Experiments show it beating DMED, KL-UCB, Bayes-UCB.
limits: Bernoulli rewards, stationary arms, independent pulls.
agent_relevance: Gives a rule with a known logarithmic cost of exploring. Stationarity fails when the agent's own prompt changes between attempts.

source: Burda et al. (2018) Large-Scale Study of Curiosity-Driven Learning
finding: Noisy-TV test: adding a random-channel TV to a Unity maze slows curiosity agents a lot, but they sometimes still reach the real reward.
numbers: Authors added a TV with a channel-change action. Text: the TV 'drastically slows down learning' of IDF and RF agents; agents sometimes converge to the extrinsic reward if run long enough.
quote: if you run the experiment for long enough the agents do sometimes converge to getting the extrinsic reward consistently
limits: Single maze; thought experiment made literal. No trial count in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Anything that scores novelty by unpredictability is pulled to noise. For text, random rephrasing is the TV. Reward branches by verifiable checks, not surprise.

source: Burda et al. (2018) Exploration by Random Network Distillation
finding: Random Network Distillation (RND) bonus reaches state-of-the-art on Montezuma's Revenge with no demonstrations.
numbers: Table 1 final mean: Montezuma RND 8,152 vs PPO 2,497 vs dynamics-based 400; Gravitar RND 3,906 vs PPO 3,426; PrivateEye RND 8,666 vs dynamics 105; Venture RND 1,859 vs dynamics 0; Pitfall! RND -3. Best agent often finds 22 of 24 rooms.
quote: an agent maximizing the RND exploration bonus consistently finds more than half of the rooms
limits: Pitfall!: both PPO and RND find no positive reward. Solaris: comparable to PPO. Gravitar: no consistent gain over PPO.
agent_relevance: An intrinsic bonus helps only in some sparse tasks; elsewhere it equals plain search. Test per class before adding it.

source: Burda et al. (2018) Exploration by Random Network Distillation
finding: Own-seed discrepancy: Montezuma results are dominated by outliers and discrete early choices.
numbers: Footnote: CNN results averaged over 5 seeds disagreed strongly with 10 seeds for the best setting; the later public code reproduced Figure 6 and authors tell others to compare to that.
limits: Heavy-tailed outcomes: one left-or-right choice in the first room decides much.
agent_relevance: Few-seed exploration results are unreliable. Judge the per-class widen rule on many runs, not 5.

source: Burda et al. (2018) Exploration by Random Network Distillation
finding: Controlled comparison: the noise-prone forward-dynamics bonus does worse than RND, the noisy-TV effect in real Atari with sticky actions.
numbers: Same CNN policy: dynamics bonus significantly worse than RND on Montezuma (400 vs 8,152), PrivateEye (105 vs 8,666) and Solaris; similar on Venture, Pitfall, Gravitar. Agent oscillated between two rooms because sticky actions make the next frame unpredictable.
quote: This is a manifestation of the 'noisy TV' problem, or aleatoric uncertainty
limits: Sticky actions are environment noise; gap is for the same code with only the prediction target changed.
agent_relevance: Separates learnable from irreducible uncertainty. A widen rule should count only reducible uncertainty (a branch a check could resolve).

source: Burda et al. (2018) Exploration by Random Network Distillation
finding: Intrinsic-reward agents get stuck 'dancing with skulls': they keep repeating risky but already-solved behaviour.
numbers: Qualitative: once known extrinsic rewards are collected, the RND agent loops over moving skulls, laser gates and disappearing bridges in Montezuma and Pitfall!.
limits: Qualitative observation; no rate given.
agent_relevance: Bonuses can outlive their use. Retire exploration for a class once checks show it is saturated.

source: Savinov et al. (2019) Episodic Curiosity through Reachability
finding: Episodic curiosity through reachability avoids the couch-potato (TV) trap and speeds up sparse goal reaching.
numbers: VizDoom MyWayHome (Dense, Sparse, Very Sparse): matches ICM on final result, reaching 100% success in all three, and reaches 100% at least 2 times faster than ICM.
quote: our method reaches 100% success rate at least 2 times faster
limits: Re-implemented ICM checked against Pathak et al. R-network pre-training budget is counted in the comparison.
agent_relevance: Novelty defined as 'many steps from anything seen' ignores randomness one step away. Text analogue: a branch is novel only if it is not a rewording of known ones.

source: Savinov et al. (2019) Episodic Curiosity through Reachability
finding: Under injected TV noise all methods get worse, but episodic curiosity stays above the baselines, and ICM can fall below plain PPO.
quote: reasonably robust to all sources of stochasticity
limits: Tables partly garbled in extraction; Image Action columns not cited. Authors' own method and own noise design.
agent_relevance: In noise settings ICM scored below plain PPO (7.7 vs 11.6). A bonus can hurt, not just fail to help.

source: Bellemare et al. (2016) Unifying Count-Based Exploration and Intrinsic Motivation
finding: Pseudo-counts from a density model link count-based exploration to intrinsic motivation and help on hard Atari games.
numbers: Abstract: pseudo-counts from raw pixels give significant exploration on hard games including Montezuma's Revenge. Exact scores not read.
limits: Read abstract and introduction only; no scores cited.
agent_relevance: Counts, not surprise, are the classic cure for noise: a noisy source gets many counts fast. Counting attempts per class is the same idea.

source: Ecoffet et al. (2019) Go-Explore: a New Approach for Hard-Exploration Problems
finding: Go-Explore archives and returns to promising states before exploring, and scores far above intrinsic-motivation agents.
numbers: Montezuma's Revenge: mean 43,763 without domain knowledge (about 4x prior state of the art); mean 666,474 with easy domain knowledge, best run over 18 million, 1,441 levels. Pitfall: mean 59,494, max 107,363 (first above zero).
limits: Phase 1 assumes a resettable or deterministic simulator; phase 2 robustifies into stochastic play.
agent_relevance: Maps to tree search: keep an archive of states, return to the best one, then explore. Cheap for text states, which can be restored exactly.

source: Ecoffet et al. (2019) Go-Explore: a New Approach for Hard-Exploration Problems
finding: Two named failure modes of intrinsic motivation: detachment (forgetting promising areas) and derailment (random perturbation destroys a return).
numbers: Paper states IM agents have two layers of exploration, and stochastic perturbation derails the agent from returning to a promising state; longer paths derail more often.
limits: Conceptual argument backed by their results, not an isolated test.
agent_relevance: Warns against widening by random noise on deep branches. Return to the exact stored state, then vary.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can Large Language Models Explore In-Context?
finding: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama2 fail to explore in bandits in almost all prompt configurations tried.
numbers: Only one config worked of those tested: GPT-4 with a hint to explore, externally summarized per-arm averages, and chain-of-thought. Basic GPT-4 prompt had suffix failures (never picking the best arm after early rounds) in more than 60% of replicates.
quote: only one configuration resulted in satisfactory exploratory behavior
limits: Bernoulli bandits (5 arms in the headline figure), horizon T=100, with T=500 check. Success needed outside code to summarize history; the same config without summary failed.
agent_relevance: Supports 'program decides, model fills slot': the model should not decide when to widen from raw history. Pass counts as statistics.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can Large Language Models Explore In-Context?
finding: LLM failure modes: greedy lock-in (suffix failure) and uniform-like picking.
numbers: Surrogate statistic SuffFailFreq(T/2): satisfactory runs need at most 15%. Only three GPT-4 configs avoided suffix failures, and two of these failed another way (uniform-like, very high MinFrac).
limits: Authors argue short horizons hide the failure; failures show at longer T.
agent_relevance: Measure widening with these two statistics: share of runs that never revisit the best class, and spread of effort across classes.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can Large Language Models Explore In-Context?
finding: Chain-of-thought alone does not fix exploration if history is not summarized.
numbers: Abstract: all other configs failed, including those with chain-of-thought but unsummarized history. Authors say external summarization is essential and may not be possible in complex settings.
limits: Small bandits only; no fine-tuning tested.
agent_relevance: Matches guardrail G1 and code-checked counters: let code keep sufficient statistics.

source: Nie et al. (2024/25) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For Exploration
finding: EVOLvE (BanditBench): summarized history beats raw history for in-context demonstrations, and UCB-based algorithm-guided support helps.
numbers: Few-shot win-rate 50.2% with summarized history vs 27.5% with raw history (MAB). Table 2 lists UCB/LinUCB at 96.4 as the reference.
limits: Gemini-1.5 and Gemma models, MAB and contextual bandits. Table columns garbled by extraction; only text-stated figures cited.
agent_relevance: Putting UCB-style scores (count plus bonus) into the prompt works better than raw history. Cheap and code-computed.

source: Nie et al. (2024/25) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For Exploration
finding: Fine-tuning on UCB trajectories lifts a small model above a larger one, and easy vs hard training tasks generalise differently for few-shot vs fine-tuning.
numbers: Few-shot win-rate 50.2 with easy-task demos vs 43.0 with hard. Fine-tuning 65.6 trained on hard vs 54.5 on easy. Best fine-tuned Gemini-1.5 Flash surpasses Gemini-1.5 Pro.
quote: the best fine-tuned Gemini-1.5 Flash model surpasses even the Gemini-1.5 Pro model
limits: Needs training; we use a scaffold only. Authors suspect fine-tuning overfits training task structure.
agent_relevance: Fine-tuning is out of scope; the in-context finding (summaries beat raw history) transfers.

source: Nie et al. (2024/25) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For Exploration
finding: Algorithm-guided support helps most when the action space is large or the task is complex.
numbers: Text: consistent gains from raw history to AG for Flash and Pro and in contextual bandits; AG helps when the number of actions is large. Few-shot RH 3.6 rose to 10.7 with RH+AG demos even when AG was absent at inference.
quote: Providing AG during inference will always increase the model's performance
limits: Win-rates are relative to other methods, not absolute reward.
agent_relevance: With many classes or branches the benefit of a code-built UCB score grows.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS)
finding: UCT tree search over LLM steps (LATS) lifts HumanEval pass@1 with GPT-4 from 80.1 to 92.7.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1: base GPT-4 80.1, LATS (ReAct) 92.7. Settings n=5 children, exploration weight w=1. On WebShop LATS beats RL-trained baselines at the same iterations.
quote: LATS achieves state-of-the-art pass@1 accuracy (92.7%) for programming on HumanEval
limits: Uses real test feedback and a model-written value score; compute much higher than one pass. Some baselines use 161 of the questions.
agent_relevance: UCT widening works when real tests exist (matches G2/G3); the gain costs extra compute.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS)
finding: Exploration weight in UCT matters on HotPotQA: lower weight hurts; higher weight does not improve accuracy but converges faster.
numbers: HotPotQA EM: w=0.5 gives 0.55; w=2.0 gives 0.63. Authors: optimal setting depends on the environment and complexity of the state space.
quote: The optimal setting depends on the particular environment and complexity of the state space
limits: One dataset, single ablation, no seed spread; table partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that exploration constants are environment dependent, supporting a per-class widen setting.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS)
finding: Every LATS component is needed on HotPotQA: DFS instead of UCT-style search, or no reflection, lowers exact match.
numbers: HotPotQA ablation EM: LATS (DFS) 0.42, LATS (no reflection) 0.58, full LATS (ReAct) 0.63.
quote: LATS requires every component and operation for optimal performance
limits: n=5 children, k=50 trajectories; one benchmark.
agent_relevance: Systematic depth-first lost 21 points to the UCT-balanced search in this one test.

source: Zhang, Lehman et al. (2024) OMNI: Open-endedness via Models of human Notions of Interestingness
finding: A foundation model as a model of interestingness picks tasks that are both learnable and interesting, beating uniform sampling and learning-progress alone.
numbers: Abstract only: FM-based MoIs improve open-ended learning, outperforming uniform task sampling and learning progress alone. Exact scores not read.
quote: outperforming baselines based on uniform task sampling or learning progress alone
limits: Read abstract and intro only; an LLM judges interest, so risk of self-preference (SCHEMA section 1).
agent_relevance: Learning progress alone chases learnable-but-boring tasks; a second filter helps. Prefer code-checked value over LLM taste.

source: Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Fischer (2002) Finite-time analysis of the multiarmed bandit problem
finding: UCB1 gives logarithmic regret uniformly over time without prior knowledge of reward distributions.
numbers: Not opened this session; from memory: UCB1 regret grows as O(ln n).
limits: Not verified here.
agent_relevance: Standard citation for the UCB widen score.

source: Chapelle & Li (2011) An Empirical Evaluation of Thompson Sampling
finding: Reported Thompson sampling competitive with or better than UCB on simulated bandits and on news recommendation.
numbers: Not opened this session; claim from memory, no numbers recorded.
limits: Not verified here. Counterpoint to Kuleshov & Precup that simple heuristics win.
agent_relevance: Two empirical studies disagree on ranking, so run both on our own data.
